text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
British economist THOMAS MALTHUS, famous for his theories that population would grow to outstrip resources, was born on this day in 1766.
The American who invented the typewriter, CHRISTOPHER SCHOLES, was born in 1819.
American journalist CARL BERNSTEIN, who exposed the "Watergate scandal" with BOB WOODWARD, was born in 1944.
British film director ALAN PARKER, ("Bugsy Malone", "Midnight Express", "Evita") was also born in 1944.
British footballer and England international player KEVIN KEEGAN was born in 1951. Keegan recently stood down as manager of English glamour club, Newcastle United.
US singer/songwriter, actor and film script writer TIM BUCKLEY was born in 1947. He was seen as one of the most innovative musicians to emerge in the latter half of the 1960s. He died in June 1975.
** EVENTS **
1400 : English King RICHARD II died mysteriously at
Pontefract Castle.
1779 : Captain JAMES COOK was killed by natives in
Hawaii, after some of his crew had started trouble with a local chief.
1803 : A mechanic named MOSES COATS invented the apple
parer.
1876 : American inventor ELISHA GRAY announced his
intention to file a patent for the telephone, just hours after such a patent was filed by ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL.
1879 : LA MARSEILLAISE officially became the French
National Anthem.
1919 : The forerunner of the United Nations, the League
of Nations, was born when delegates from 27 nations agreed to US President WOODROW WILSON's proposal for a "general association".
1924 : The "labour-saving" cooking device, the casserole,
went on sale in Melbourne.
1929 : Seven men from "Bugs" MORAN's gang were

gunned-down in a Chicago garage. Five gunmen, three wearing police uniforms and all thought to have been members of AL 'Scarface' CAPONE's gang, lined the seven up against a wall and opened fire. At the time, almost half the Chicago Police Force was under investigation for corruption. The incident became known as the "St Valentine's Day Massacre".
1938 : Nineteen people drowned in Sydney Harbour when an

overcrowded ferry capsized. The "Rodney" was carrying 175 people to farewell the US cruiser "Louisville". The vessel rolled when the passengers gathered on one side to get a close look at the American ship. Members of a police band and US sailors jumped in to rescue the passengers while others threw in lifeboats. Several people were trapped in the launch. A little under a month later the Sydney Coroner's court returned a finding of accidental death in the disaster.
1946 : An "electronic brain" took seconds to do

mathematical calculations that would take a human hours. The ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was operating at the University of Pennsylvania. The "brain" was described as more than a mere adding machine with a memory and a capacity to be "programmed". The machine was reported as having 18,000 electronic valves but no moving parts.
1966 : Australia changed to decimal currency. Some small
shops avoided the first day of conversion by not opening. But according to the Chairman of the Decimal Currency Board there was very little chaos and was in fact seen by some as an anti-climax.
1973 : An Israeli fighter-jet shot-down a Libyan
passenger plane over the Sinai Desert, killing 74 people.
1977 : Nine Gippsland schoolchildren and their teacher

were abducted by an escaped prisoner. The escapee, EDWARD JOHN EASTWOOD, was serving 15 years for kidnapping six Victorian schoolchildren and their teacher in 1972. In his second mass kidnapping EASTWOOD took the young teacher, the children aged six to 11, and five other hostages to a well prepared bush hideout. EASTWOOD was shot and captured after a hostage escaped and called police from a farmhouse.
1989 : Iranian leader AYATOLLAH KHOMEINI condemned
British author SALMAN RUSHDIE to death for blasphemy, over his book "The Satanic Verses".
1994 : Victoria's STEVE MONEGHETTI won the Tokyo marathon
in freezing conditions, running during the heaviest sonwfall in the city in 25 years.
